History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
40-year-old woman with childhood asthma presents with 2-day history of progressive wheeze and shortness of breath following dust exposure while cleaning; advised to attend GP clinic for assessment, pulse oximetry, possible antihistamine and steroid therapy.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath.  
• Onset: Began ~2 days ago, ~1 hour after vigorous house-cleaning with significant dust exposure.  
• Course: Persistent for 48 hours; worsening, particularly at night.  
• Severity/impact: Feels “a bit short of breath”; sometimes unable to complete sentences during conversation; no chest pain with deep inspiration.  
• Exacerbating factors: Night-time; presumed dust exposure.  
• Relieving factors: None tried; has not used inhaler or other medication.  
• Associated symptoms: No dizziness, no chest pain, no systemic symptoms reported.  
• Fluid intake: ~4–5 glasses of water daily.  

Review of systems: Only respiratory symptoms elicited; remainder not explored in transcript.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – childhood onset; largely quiescent but occasional exercise-induced episodes; owns a short-acting inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented); has required oral steroids in the past.  
• Seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever) – summer months; no regular medication.  

Medications:
• Salbutamol (presumed) inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented; not used for current episode.  
• No current antihistamines; none other stated.

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies reported.

Social History:
• Living situation: At home during consult (further details not provided).  
• Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs: Not discussed.  
• Access to care: ~10-minute drive to GP surgery.  
• Financial: Can purchase OTC antihistamine (£4–6).

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Not performed in virtual consult.  
• No vitals available.

Investigations:
• None performed yet.  
• Planned: Pulse oximetry at GP clinic to assess oxygen saturation; further tests as needed.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected asthma exacerbation vs dust-induced allergic reaction  
  • Assessment: Wheeze, SOB after dust exposure; past asthma and hay fever history.  
  • Plan:  
    – Attend GP/urgent care clinic today for in-person assessment and pulse oximetry.  
    – Consider nebulized or inhaled bronchodilator if wheeze significant.  
    – Consider oral corticosteroid course if objective asthma exacerbation confirmed.  
    – Start nonsedating antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine) OTC en route if available.  
    – Provide letter via app summarizing teleconsult for GP.

General plan items:  
• Education on trigger avoidance (dust).  
• Advise to bring current inhaler to appointment; update prescriptions as needed.  
• Seek emergency help if worsening breathlessness, inability to speak, or chest tightness.  
• Follow up after GP visit as directed.

Quality checks:

Missing but clinically expected elements:  
• Detailed allergy status, complete medication reconciliation, smoking/alcohol history, vitals, lung auscultation findings, peak flow, past hospital admissions for asthma.

Internal conflicts: None noted.

Transcript quality: Clear; minor drop in video but audio preserved.
